item.title: REVIEW: Biwin M560 2TB SSD Review: The DRAM-less drive to beat
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The Biwin M560 is one of the best all-around PCIe 5.0 SSDs we’ve tested, with class-leading responsiveness and excellent efficiency. - +Top-tier application and gaming performance Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. We’re back with another drive from Biwin, which has been putting out some good SSDs with minor exceptions. This one uses hardware we’ve wanted to test in retail for quite some time: the SMI SM2504XT SSD controller, which is hard to find. The PCIe 5.0 DRAM-less range is relatively popular because it offers the performance without the power and heat of higher-end options, at a lower price point. The tech’s newer than what PCIe 4.0 drives offer, so you get a better all-around experience if you’re willing to take the plunge. The M560 slots in here perfectly as a real alternative to all the drives in this class with Phison hardware. The Biwin M560 is available only in 1TB and 2TB capacities. Is that a disappointment? It’s normal to expect at least 4TB SKUs these days, but 8TB is certainly a bridge too far for a four-channel controller. Yes, we have some 8TB DRAM-less drives floating around, but for the most part you can’t find those units. 4TB is more common and highly desired — this is what makes the Lexar NM790 so legendary — but it actually is a decent amount of flash for this type of controller. With the ideal amount of flash for this controller being four dies per channel, or 16 total, 2TB really is the sweet spot. So we’re fine with that for this drive, even if it is higher-end. Right now the drive can be found for $189.99 and $364.99 for the two SKUs, which is not unreasonably priced for the hardware. At 2TB, it is right in line with the Crucial P510, for example. It’s also below the top drives with DRAM, like the Samsung 9100 Pro, by enough that it makes sense. You can get PCIe 5.0 DRAM SSDs at around this price or cheaper, but you’re giving up some things to do so, which we’ll get into later. The drive is rated for up to 11,000 / 10,000 MB/s for sequential reads and writes and up to a whopping 1,700K / 1,700K random read and write IOPS. 1.7 million IOPS! That’s astounding, and even exceeds the 1.3+ million, on paper, from direct competitor Phison E31T-based drives, like the Corsair MP700 Elite. This thing is a beast for a DRAM-less drive. Biwin doesn’t skimp on the warranty, either. It’s the typical five-year affair for duration, but you’re covered for up to 750TB of writes for every TB of space. This is 25% more than is typical, if you care about that sort of thing. We consider it a bonus. Hitting the download tab for the M560’s site shows three downloads available: the Biwin Data Recovery Tool for macOS, one for Windows, and Biwin Intelligence. The first two are pretty self-explanatory, but we will give kudos to Biwin for having the macOS option. For the last, it is the company’s SSD toolbox, which is an all-in-one software solution dashboard you can use to check your drive’s health, update firmware, and so forth. Biwin lists the supported functions on its page. The toolbox only supports Windows at this time. The Biwin M560 is, as expected, a single-sided drive, which we prefer. Less that can go wrong, fits into more machines, and can be easier to cool. The top label is heat-spreading. The back label has drive information, including the 3.3 V / 2.0 A rating, which puts the drive power draw below about 7W. According to the S.M.A.R.T. report, the maximum power draw is 8W. These numbers might be concerning, especially as good DRAM-less SSDs tend to be at around 6.5W or less. Well, as it turns out, the drive is much more comfortable at 4W, with a maximum significantly below 6.5W and an average of one-half that, as you can explore in more detail with our power testing. Even very efficient PCIe 5.0 drives tend to step up over the last generation, making heat something to watch in some cases. Not in this one — we think this will be great in laptops, and exceptionally cool in PCIe 4.0 ones. The components don’t even take up half of the PCB space! Impressive engineering, and the extra spacing between components can help spread heat. Here we have one controller, the SMI SM2504XT, which we previously covered in an ES preview, and two NAND flash packages. The controller performed exceptionally in our preview testing and is more than a match for the best controllers out there, whether Phison’s competing E31T or even many drives with DRAM such as those based on the E26. The flash, in this case, is Kioxia’s 218-layer BiCS8 TLC, which is also exceptional. This flash has excellent latency and is also power-efficient. This combination is a match made in heaven, and it’s a shame we don’t see the SM2504XT more often.

item.title: SALES: Travel gifts: 24 thoughtful Christmas presents for the globetrotter in your life
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Whether you are shopping for a seasoned jet-setter, a frequent long-haul flyer, or someone simply planning their next weekend getaway, finding the perfect gift for a travel lover is all about balancing stylish design with clever, stress-reducing functionality. At Condé Nast Traveller, we spend serious time on the road testing everything from luggage to inflight accessories – meaning we know exactly which pieces are genuinely worth giving. To help you take the guesswork out of your festive shopping, we’ve rounded up our ultimate editor-approved travel gifts. Inside this definitive guide, you’ll find space-saving packing hacks, ultra-comfortable flight pillows, and surprisingly aesthetic phone chargers alongside timeless leather accessories, iconic coffee-table books, and jetset beauty staples. Each of these travel essentials has been hand-picked by our team for its durability, design, and practical charm, ensuring your loved ones will travel in style, wherever their wanderlust takes them next. Our editors’ top picks of the best travel gifts for 2026 These are the tried-and-tested gifts our editors genuinely use, love and recommend – and we’re confident you’ll love them too. But what new goodies do our editors want to find under the tree themselves? See our own wishlists in our round-up for 2026. Every item in this gifts for travellers guide has earned its place through rigorous, real-world testing by our team of seasoned editors. As frequent flyers who spend much of the year on the move, we don’t just recommend products based on how they look on a shelf – we take them on long-haul flights, pack them into overhead lockers, drag them along cobblestones and put them through their paces on everything from quick weekenders to long-haul assignments. From checking the smooth roll of a carry-on’s wheels to ensuring a sleep mask stays comfortable for eight hours at 30,000 feet, we only include the travel gear, tech and accessories that we genuinely rely on ourselves and love enough to give to our own friends and family. As a travel and commerce writer for Condé Nast Traveller for the last three years, plus a further four-year stint writing shopping guides for Good Housekeeping, I have tested hundreds of products – so I know how to find the best of the best. I spend a large portion of my time living out of a suitcase, trialling gear on the move – I tend to take at least one flight a month. It means my recommendations are grounded in hands-on experience, with most products tried out over a considerable length of time.

item.title: SALES: The 10 best places to visit in November 2026
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
November is peak shoulder season: The weather can be unpredictable (but you can get really lucky), crowds are small nearly everywhere and prices are often the lowest they'll be all year for many destinations. It is an ideal time to travel in many ways, if you're willing to risk less-than-ideal weather in some places. Thanksgiving also takes place in the U.S., and if you are not obligated to visit family, you can enjoy a wonderful four-day vacation without missing any school or work. And for those who love Christmas markets and lights, several spots start their displays at the end of the month. Here are 10 great destinations to consider for your November getaway. Marrakech and the Atlas Mountains, Morocco This stunning desert and mountain region enjoys cooler weather in November that’s ideal for hiking in the Atlas Mountains. Meanwhile, the nearby city of Marrakech is as vibrant as ever, with more people coming out in the less-than-scorching temps that linger all summer. Wander the souk, stroll the gorgeous gardens, and visit architectural highlights without breaking a sweat. Nov. 18 is Morocco's Independence Day, and this year’s Marrakech Coffee & Tea Festival will run Nov. 5-7, with more than 400 exhibitors and various workshops and classes. This year’s Marrakech International Film Festival runs from Nov. 20–28. Use points to stay at the Park Hyatt Marrakech, which opened in 2025 (rates from $594 or 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night), or check out the new Riad Beij, in the heart of the Medina (rates from $168 per night). To stay in the Atlas Mountains, you can use Virgin Red points at the luxe Virgin Limited Edition Kasbah Tamadot (rates from $577 or 140,000 Virgin Red points per night). TPG tip: Marrakech has increased seasonal direct flight access, including a direct flight from Newark on United Airlines, which launched in 2024, and from Atlanta on Delta Air Lines, which debuted at the end of 2025. Oaxaca's celebration of Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is legendary, especially in Oaxaca City, where festivities and commemorations take place every year from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2. Expect elaborate costumes, parades, street festivals, cemetery and altar visits, and plenty of music, food and drinks. After the city festivities, plan to stay at one of the region’s design-forward hotels. Boutique hotel 7 Casa Laurel opened in April this year, and Casa Yati opened in Ventanilla on the beach last summer. La Valise Mazunte is a member of Small Luxury Hotels of the World with just six suites and a villa (rates from $400 or 130,000 Hilton Honors points per night). TPG tip: You can fly directly to Puerto Escondido on United Airlines' Houston-to-Puerto Escondido route, which debuted in 2025. American Airlines launched its direct flights to Puerto Escondido from Dallas-Fort Worth in December 2025. November is the very beginning of the dry season in Thailand, so it's a good time to beat the winter crowds and score good airfare and hotel pricing. Nov. 24 is Loy Krathong, the beautiful floating lantern festival that lights up the Bangkok waterways on the night of the full moon in the 12th month of the Thai lunar calendar. Various events happen along the Chao Phraya River, in public parks and at cultural landmarks. The city, which has several new hotels this year, with something for almost every loyalist. Voco Bangkok Surawong opened in January 2026 (rates from 19,000 IHG One Rewards and $137 per night). Canopy by Hilton Bangkok Sukhumvit opened in August 2026 (rates from 45,000 Hilton Honors points and $170 per night). The long-delayed Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit finally opened, also in August, with LEED Gold certification, a jasmine-inspired spa, seven food and beverage outlets and 474 rooms (rates from 12,345 ALL Accor points and $278 per night). TPG tip: Last year, United Airlines launched a new daily flight to Bangkok via Hong Kong from Los Angeles and San Francisco, making it the only domestic airline to offer a daily one-stop flight to Bangkok from the U.S. Looking for an adventure? November is the last month of the dry season to visit the Amazon, so there's still time to squeeze in an adventure before the end of the year. If colorful birds, jaguars, river dolphins and caiman sightings aren't enough for you, the first-ever Global Citizen music festival in the Amazon, in Belem, is Nov. 1. Global Citizen Festival Amazonia brings Brazilian music stars Anitta, Seu Jorge and Gaby Amarantos and Coldplay's Chris Martin together with Indigenous leaders to amplify climate action campaigns. TPG tip: Avianca flies to Belem via Bogota, Colombia, from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), and LATAM flies there through Sao Paulo/Guarulhos International Airport (GRU). Book a room at Ibis Styles Belem Batista Campos ($67 per night) or Grand Mercure Belem do Para ($474 per night). Both are members of Accor Live Limitless. If you've dreamed of a vacation in St. Barts but thought you couldn't afford it, November may be the best time to visit the gorgeous Caribbean island. You'll enjoy warm weather, beat the winter crowds and enjoy better prices on hotels and flights. And while the French island is known for always having excellent food, November brings even more culinary star power to the isle. The Saint-Barth Gourmet Festival is Nov. 9-15 and features five chefs from Michelin-starred restaurants, including chef Amaury Bouhours of Restaurant Le Meurice Alain Ducasse and Thibault Sombardier of Les Parisiens. TPG tip: Getting to St. Barts can be a bit of a journey if you don't have a private jet (ahem), but Cape Air flies twice daily from well-connected St. Thomas. Looking to the other hemisphere is always a good idea, and in Australia, they're experiencing the other shoulder season: spring. In Western Australia, this means gorgeous wildflowers and some excellent festivals worth traveling for. Foodies should plan to attend the world-renowned Pair'd Margaret River Region food and wine festival (Nov. 19-22), which brings world-class wine, food and music to the Margaret River region. This year's lineup includes chefs Rodney Scott, Matt Abe, and Mindy Woods, as well as wine writer Erin Larkin. TPG tip: Hyde Perth opened in March of this year (rates from $239 per night) as the first Hyde hotel in Australia, a brand from Ennismore (also behind the Hoxton, Mama Shelter, Delano, and 25Hours brands) that also has locations in London, Ibiza, Dubai, and Miami. Some November trips require compromising on the weather, but not in the desert. Palm Springs in November is ideal: With a daytime high of 79 degrees Fahrenheit and a low of 52 degrees Fahrenheit at night, you’ll still avoid its peak tourist months, which begin in January. It’s also ideal weather to hike in nearby Joshua Tree National Park. Though most Pride events occur in June, the Palm Springs Pride Festival is a fall event. This year, it runs from Nov. 6–8, with the big parade on the final day. Expect live music, comedy, local vendors and artists, and plenty of food and drink stands in several areas across the downtown area. The Sunset Music and Comedy Festival runs concurrently each night at the Agua Caliente Casino. There are several new and improved attractions in the desert: The Palm Springs Air Museum recently completed a $2.5 million renovation, and reopened in September, featuring a turbine-inspired façade, new exhibits, and the Ronald M. Auen Learning Center, and DSRT Surf, a manmade surf lagoon that creates the perfect wave, every time, opened this summer in Palm Desert. TPG tip: The iconic La Quinta Resort & Club celebrates its centennial in 2026, with special events and guest experiences all year long. It’s now a part of Hilton’s Curio Collection, so you can use and earn rewards points there (rates from 85,000 Hilton Honors points and $329 per night) Florence in summer can be a hot, crowded mess, but come November, there are fewer crowds and mild weather (although rain is likely). It's also truffle-hunting season in Tuscany. Film lovers should mark Oct. 31-Nov. 8 for the Festival dei Popoli, Europe's oldest international documentary film festival. And Nov. 29 brings runners from around the world to the Estra Firenze Marathon. Finally, most Christmas markets open around the city in the last week of November. TPG tip: The city recently welcomed Borgo Pignano Florence, set on a 5-acre estate with 11 historic buildings and 32 rooms and is part of Relais & Chateaux. La Resérve Firenze opened Oct. 15 inside a restored 15th-century palazzo. If you want to use points, W Florence (rates from $507 or 70,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night) opened last year. Rev your engines for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, when Formula 1 racing comes to Sin City from Nov. 19-21. Outside the hugely popular event, you can find some hotel and flight deals this November. And there's still plenty to do in November beyond F1. At the Sphere, you can catch the 4D version of "The Wizard of Oz" daily throughout the month, or see Metallica Nov. 4-7, the Eagles Nov. 13-14 and 27-28. Christmas also starts early in Vegas on Nov. 5, when the 3-acre Cactus Garden at Ethel M Chocolate Factory opens its annual lights show, and Nov. 14 at the Bellagio Conservatory, where they pull out all the stops to create a lit-up floral winter wonderland. Foodies should also be excited: Taylor Swift favorite and NYC hotspot The Corner Store is opening its second location at the Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas on November 9. TPG tip: United restored its nonstop service between Cleveland and Las Vegas in September, with five flights a week and budget airline Breeze Airways added a daily route between Las Vegas and John Wayne Airport in Orange County. November is the tail end of hurricane season so the possibilities of one hitting are slim—and there are great deals to be had, and usually, excellent weather. Miches — located on the northeast coast of the Dominican Republic — has been increasing its number of high-end all-inclusive resorts, and it’s typically much less crowded than Punta Cana, which is near the airport. Hilton loyalists can turn Hilton Honors points into an all-inclusive stay at Zemi Miches Punta Cana All-Inclusive Resort, Hilton's first Curio Collection all-inclusive resort in the country. Hyatt has also planted its all-inclusive flag in Miches with two openings: Dreams Playa Esmeralda Resort & Spa and Secrets Playa Esmeralda Resort & Spa. At Dreams, families and kids are welcome to enjoy the beautiful beaches, pools, and many restaurants and bars, while Secrets is adults-only. TPG tip: No matter where you stay, let the hotel arrange your transportation from Punta Cana International Airport for ease and affordability. The transportation area at this airport can be overwhelming, and after a long flight, who doesn't want everything made easy? Related reading:

item.title: REVIEW: Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HS 6K Gaming Monitor Review: I Wish You Were an OLED
item.description:
Source: PCMag
A 4K resolution (3,840 by 2,160 pixels) has long been the practical ceiling for premium gaming monitors. (Try running your AAA games at good frame rates higher than that!) But technology relentlessly marches onward, so it's time for more pixels. Like the few TVs that have offered 8K resolution (and since moved away from that target), just a few gaming monitors have exceeded 4K, and those under limited circumstances, such as ultrawide displays like the Alienware 39 5K OLED. Enter the Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HS 6K ($1,599), the world’s first 32-inch 6K gaming monitor. It offers rock-solid gaming performance atop a sky-high resolution. Gamers with top-of-the-line desktop PCs might find this monitor worth a close look, but most people should skip it. The bump up from 4K resolution is impressive technically, but many gamers won't find it worth it. Add in a ho-hum contrast ratio compared with OLED competitors, a lack of USB-C ports, and a high asking price, and you'd be better off with our top premium gaming monitor pick, the Asus ROG Swift PG27UCDM. The G80HS is a 32-inch monitor measuring 23.4 by 28.1 by 10.4 inches (HWD) and weighing 16.3 pounds with the stand. That makes it considerably lighter than older 32-inch monitors like the HP Omen Transcend 32 OLED and the Asus ROG Swift OLED PG32UCDM, which both weigh 19.4 pounds with their stand factored in. Standing firmly on a pentagonal base, the G80HS proves quite flexible, with ample tilt and swivel options. The screen also offers a full 90-degree pivot, which is helpful for dealing with text-heavy documentation. It also adds an additional layer of flexibility that people who use multi-screen configurations will surely appreciate—vertical orientation saves a lot of space on your desk when you've got two or more monitors. Turning the monitor around to examine its port hub, you’ll find two HDMI 2.1 ports, a DisplayPort 2.1, two USB Type-A ports, a USB Type-B upstream connector, and a headphone jack. You won't find built-in speakers, and perhaps more disappointingly, you won't find any USB Type-C ports. Still, what’s available amounts to a decent mix of connectivity options. (Also missing: a built-in virtual KVM switch, which many premium gaming monitors offer to make them better for multi-input use cases.) At a glance, the G80HS is pretty simple-looking. The circle carved around the monitor’s VESA mount on the back of the cabinet adds a touch of RGB lighting. It supports Samsung CoreSync, so the monitor can sync up to the game you're playing, casting a soft, ambient wash of colors against the wall behind the screen. CoreSync doesn't have per-game support and customization like Razer's Chroma Studio, but it does attempt to mimic the game's on-screen colors. Moving toward the bottom right of the monitor, you’ll find the monitor’s OSD control stick and power button. Overall, the monitor has style, but it isn't as “loud” as other gaming monitors, especially when compared with the elaborate, sometimes gaudy cabinet-back designs of Asus monitors like the ROG Swift PG34WCDN. (That may be a good thing to you.) The first 32-inch 6K gaming monitor uses a Fast IPS panel. While that means the monitor doesn’t enjoy the rich color and inky blacks that OLED panels offer, IPS panels typically maintain higher sustained brightness compared with OLEDs. They also aren't marred by common OLED pain points such as burn-in, text fringing, and higher prices. (That said, we have seen a recent string of more-affordable OLED panels, for example, the Alienware 27 240Hz QD-OLED.) Fast IPS panels differ from standard IPS monitors by offering faster pixel response times, typically resulting in reduced motion blur and ghosting. In my experience, however, the difference between Fast IPS and IPS is small at best and mostly a marketing play. With that being said, this monitor doesn’t look bad in motion and offers a wide viewing angle of 178 degrees, so you’d be hard-pressed to find an angle that doesn’t look good while playing. But the G80HS is not just a pretty face; it also promises impressive performance for high-refresh play. The monitor has two distinct picture modes: 6K at up to a 165Hz refresh rate, and 3K at up to 330Hz. The 6K mode is meant for single-player games, while the 3K mode is aimed at gamers interested in multiplayer games and competitive play. The peak refresh rate of 330Hz is not as high as the 500Hz of MSI’s MPG 271QR QD-OLED X50, and a far cry from the 1,000Hz of monitors like LG UltraGear 25G590B-B. But remember that these and most other ultra-high-refresh monitors sacrifice resolution to reach those targets—1080p, in the LG's case. They're also not as big as the G80HS. That makes the 330Hz at 3K resolution even more impressive. The monitor also supports AMD FreeSync Premium and is Nvidia G-Sync Compatible to prevent screen tearing and lag. We put the G80HS through our standard benchmark tests using Portrait Displays' Calman calibration software and a Klein K-10A colorimeter. I also ran it through a gauntlet of games to measure input lag and judge its real-world performance. The test results below are with out-of-the-box settings, unless otherwise noted. In the first test, we benchmarked the display brightness using the out-of-the-box SDR profile. Under these conditions, we measured a maximum brightness of 434 nits with a 10% window size, exceeding the monitor’s maximum rated brightness of 400 nits. So far, so good. HDR brightness paints a similar rosy picture. We recorded 444 nits at a 10% window size. Interestingly, the monitor does not have an official high-tier VESA DisplayHDR certification. Samsung doesn't offer a reason for this, but my guess is that since IPS panels naturally have lower native contrast ratios and visible backlight glow, it would be difficult to hit the deep black levels mandated by VESA testing. The monitor does support HDR10+, though, which optimizes brightness and contrast when you're playing a supported game. We also tested the color gamut coverage. Our metering indicates that the G80HS covers 91.4% of the Adobe RGB color space (see the chart above), 127.9% of the sRGB color space, and 95.2% of the DCI-P3 color space (see the chart below). The squares represent target color reference points, and the circles represent the actual measured color. It exceeds 100% sRGB, which happens less frequently in non-OLED monitors than in OLED ones. While a wider gamut can produce richer colors, especially with HDR content, it can also sometimes lead to an overblown image. The G80HS has a rated static contrast ratio of 1,000:1, a stark difference from the essentially infinite contrast of OLED monitors like the Alienware 34 280Hz QD-OLED (AW3426DW) and the ROG Swift PG34WCDN. However, when we measured it, we found that the contrast could exceed the rating. Using Calman’s sequential contrast ratio test, which measures a display's peak white luminance and minimum black luminance, one after the other, to calculate its total dynamic range, we got a reading of 6,222:1. Still, that pales in comparison to what even the least expensive OLED gaming monitor can offer. The AW2726DM is rated for a contrast ratio of 1,500,000:1, for instance. And as you'll see below, the difference really matters in real-world use. Moving on to game testing, we used the Leo Bodnar 4K Input Lag Tester to measure the lag times of the Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HS 6K across various combinations of refresh rate and resolution. Low input lag is critical for hard-core gaming and esports, but you can benefit from it even if you're a casual gamer. The results we gathered were from the 6K/165Hz mode; we couldn't get the Bodnar to work with the 3K/330Hz mode, which is due to a limitation of the device rather than any issue with the monitor. At 1080p/60Hz, we recorded 8.4ms of input lag, and at 1080p/120Hz, 4.4ms. (We'd ordinarily test at 1080p/240Hz, too, but that was not accessible due to the 3K/330Hz mode not playing nice with the meter.) At 1440p/60Hz, we also measured 4.4ms, and at 4K/60Hz, we saw 8.6 ms of lag. We couldn't measure lag at 1,440p/120Hz, again likely due to an issue with the Bodnar device rather than the monitor. This Odyssey comes in with lower input lag times versus recent gaming monitors we’ve reviewed, like the Gigabyte MO27Q28G, the Alienware AW2726DM, and the ROG Swift PG34WCDN. These low input lag times really matter when playing shooters like Marvel Rivals, and though we don't have the meter-measured results to back it up, anecdotally, I could feel the difference when I switched to the 330Hz mode. Playing games at 6K resolution is no easy feat, as you’ll need an exceptionally powerful GPU and CPU to render all those pixels. For testing, I decided to play Cyberpunk 2077 and Pragmata, cranking up the visuals as high as possible, using our RTX 5090-equipped gaming testbed. The results looked excellent, but they also highlight the panel's dull contrast ratio. After staring at OLED monitors for so long in both my personal and professional life, I found myself missing the deep black and bright highlights of an OLED panel. Yes, on paper, the 6K resolution is better than the Alienware AW3225QF 4K QD-OLED I use as my main gaming monitor at home, but I definitely prefer my OLED. Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HS 6K Gaming Monitor - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. At $1,599, the Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HS is a pricey endeavor, with limited appeal outside of gamers with premium desktops and muscle-bound GPUs. It's also let down by an IPS panel with noticeably lower contrast in the OLED world that today's gamers inhabit. If you’re dead set on maxing out your monitor’s output or future-proofing for another line of even more powerful (and even more expensive) GPUs, the Odyssey G8 G80HS is certainly an interesting investment.
